# Trajectory Learning Principles {.unnumbered}

Parts II through IV built closure around a fixed model. @Sec-vol3-evaluation ended Part IV by measuring task acceptance and comparing configurations, then testing explanations for failures under declared conditions. Part V changes the model itself. Training changes the proposals the runtime receives. It moves none of the H·S·A exposures, grants no authority, and removes none of the runtime's enforcement obligations. A changed policy can still alter the realized trajectory length, state use, and requested effects, so its behavior needs evaluation under those same contracts. The intervention ladder of @sec-vol3-flywheel-intervention-order places training after cheaper and more reversible changes to context, tools, and the runtime, as a default order that diagnostic evidence can shorten rather than a sequence every failure must climb. Curation decides which recorded trajectories support a particular learning use, and the training objective then decides which of their tokens the model is asked to reproduce. Held-out evaluation and release policies govern whether the resulting model may replace the one in service.

::: {#pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training .callout-principle title="Verified trajectory post-training"}

**Invariant**: A recorded outcome does not determine how a trajectory should be used for learning. Curation relates the evidence to a proposed behavior change, admits records for a declared use, and distinguishes admissible targets from contextual or rejected actions. For imitation, delivered observations condition the selected responses but are not themselves targets. The objective applies to examples with at least one admitted target token. With a mask $\PositionLossMask_{t}$ that equals one only at the admitted policy-token positions of a serialized example $\SequenceToken_1,\ldots,\SequenceToken_{\SequenceLength}$ and $\ActiveTargetTokenCount=\sum_t \PositionLossMask_{t}$, the objective makes that selection exact:
$$ \MaskedFinetuningLoss(\ModelParameters) = -\frac{1}{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}\sum_{t=2}^{\SequenceLength} \PositionLossMask_{t} \log \Policy(\SequenceToken_t \mid \TokenPrefix) $$
Masked context still shapes gradients through the predictions that depend on it.

**Implication**: Passing a task check does not make every action in its trace a suitable demonstration, and recovery demonstrations cover post-error states that an error-free corpus lacks. The active-token fraction sets the supervision each trajectory supplies. Construct the mask from the admitted target spans and the actual serialized input, not from authorship alone, and evaluate the resulting policy under the intended serving format. Predicting observation tokens would add a different objective; it would not turn generated text into authentic tool evidence. @Sec-vol3-flywheel-gap and @sec-vol3-flywheel-curation develop admission, and @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-loss-masking develops the objective (@eq-vol3-sft-masked-objective).

:::

Imitation learns from selected responses, while preference learning compares assessed alternatives. Reinforcement learning instead collects new interactions and uses their rewards to guide policy updates, which turns a check into an optimization target. The verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) governs that step. When true success is rare, a small false-accept rate in the verifier makes rewarded failures a large share of the rewarded rollouts (@eq-vol3-rlvr-false-accept-share), so the assessment must stay protected from the candidate and scoped to what it checks.

The three chapters build from evidence selection to policy updates without prescribing a mandatory sequence of training methods. @Sec-vol3-trajectory-curation establishes which records and fixtures support a declared learning use. @Sec-vol3-fine-tuning turns admitted material into selected prediction targets or justified preference comparisons and an identified candidate policy. @Sec-vol3-rlvr adds fresh reward-scored interactions on states no demonstration covers, and develops the reward, the credit assigned across turns, the isolation of the verifier, and the rollout fleet that together decide what the update learns and what it costs. The policy improves only as far as the scope and protection of its check allow. Changed weights can alter behavior, not grant authority. Part VI uses a measured single-agent configuration as the baseline for deciding whether coordination is worth its cost.
